focus: Exodus 13 gathers the lasting meaning of the exodus into the consecration of the firstborn and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, so that every generation will tell how the LORD brought them out by strength of hand. The chapter then follows Israel’s first steps on the road, as God leads them the long way through the wilderness, Moses carries Joseph’s bones, and the LORD goes before them in the pillar of cloud and fire.

sections.title: The LORD Claims Every Firstborn
sections.summary: The LORD commands Moses, “Consecrate to Me all the firstborn” (Exodus 13:2), whether of man or beast. Every firstborn among the children of Israel belongs to Him.

sections.title: Remember This Day with Unleavened Bread
sections.summary: Moses tells the people to remember the day they came out of the house of bondage and to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the land the LORD gives them. Each father is to tell his son, “This is done because of what the LORD did for me when I came up from Egypt” (Exodus 13:8), and the practice will be a sign on the hand and a memorial between the eyes.

sections.title: Redeeming the Firstborn as a Testimony
sections.summary: In the land Israel is to set apart every firstborn male animal to the LORD, redeem the firstborn of a donkey with a lamb, and redeem every firstborn son. When a son asks, “What is this?” (Exodus 13:14), the father will explain that the LORD killed Egypt’s firstborn when Pharaoh refused, and that by strength of hand He brought Israel out.

sections.title: God Leads Israel by the Wilderness Way in Cloud and Fire
sections.summary: God leads the people by the wilderness of the Red Sea rather than the near road through Philistine land, lest they see war and return to Egypt, and Moses takes Joseph’s bones as Joseph had asked. The LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, and He does not take either pillar away from before the people.

1.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses after bringing Israel out of Egypt. The new instructions grow directly out of the night of deliverance.
1.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,”

The chapter opens with new instructions. Israel has just left Egypt (12:51), and God at once tells Moses how the people are to remember what He has done.

2.brief: The LORD commands, “Consecrate to Me all the firstborn,” both of man and beast, saying, “it is Mine.” Because God spared Israel’s firstborn when He struck Egypt’s, every firstborn in Israel belongs to Him.
2.explain:
“Consecrate to Me all the firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of man and beast;”

To “consecrate” means to set apart as holy, belonging to God. The phrase “whatever opens the womb” describes the first offspring a mother bears. Here God states His claim broadly, “both of man and beast.” Verses 12–15 then show how the law worked in practice: the firstborn males of the animals belonged to the LORD, and among the people it was the firstborn sons who were redeemed (13:12–13, 15).

“it is Mine.”

God gives the reason in a few words. On the night of judgment, God struck Egypt’s firstborn and spared Israel’s (12:12–13). The firstborn who lived now belong to Him. Numbers 3:13 states the reason directly: when God struck Egypt’s firstborn, “I sanctified to Myself all the firstborn in Israel.”
2.notes:
The Hebrew verb translated “consecrate” means to make holy or set apart. It is related to the word for “holy” used throughout the law.

Later God took the Levites in place of Israel’s firstborn sons for service at the tabernacle (Numbers 3:11–13, 40–51).

3.brief: Moses tells the people, “Remember this day in which you went out of Egypt,” because the LORD brought them out by strength of hand, and no leavened bread is to be eaten. The day of departure is to be remembered as the LORD’s mighty work.
3.explain:
“And Moses said to the people: ‘Remember this day in which you went out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage;”

Moses tells the people to “remember this day.” Egypt was “the house of bondage,” literally the house of slaves. The day they left it must never be forgotten.

“for by strength of hand the LORD brought you out of this place.”

The deliverance was not Israel’s own doing. The phrase “strength of hand” pictures God’s power at work against Egypt. The phrase returns three more times in this chapter (13:9, 14, 16).

“No leavened bread shall be eaten.”

The remembrance is tied to the bread. Unleavened bread recalls the haste of the night they left (12:34, 39).

4.brief: Moses reminds them that they are going out on this day, in the month Abib. The month of the exodus is marked so that its remembrance can be kept.
4.explain:
“On this day you are going out, in the month Abib.”

Moses names the month: “Abib.” The name means fresh ears of grain, the season of early harvest in spring. The exodus is fixed in time so that its remembrance can return every year.
4.notes: Abib was later called Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1). It falls in March–April.

5.brief: When the LORD brings them into the land He swore to their fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey, they are to keep this service in this month. The feast looks ahead to life in the promised land.
5.explain:
“And it shall be, when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites and the Hittites and the Amorites and the Hivites and the Jebusites,”

Moses looks ahead to the land. Five peoples are named who live there. Israel has just left Egypt, yet Moses speaks of the land as certain. The LORD “brings you,” and He will finish what He began.

“which He swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey,”

The land was sworn to the fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Genesis 15:18–21; 26:3; 28:13). “A land flowing with milk and honey” describes rich pasture for flocks and abundant produce. God had used the same words at the burning bush (3:8, 17).

“that you shall keep this service in this month.”

In the land they will keep “this service.” The feast is not only for the wilderness. It will mark Israel’s life in the land God gives.

6.brief: For seven days they are to eat unleavened bread, and the seventh day is a feast to the LORD. The week of unleavened bread ends with a celebration before Him.
6.explain:
“Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD.”

The week of unleavened bread repeats the instructions given in 12:15–20. The seventh day is a “feast to the LORD,” a celebration before Him. The week ends in joy.

7.brief: Unleavened bread is to be eaten seven days, and no leaven may be seen anywhere in their territory. The whole land is to be free of leaven during the feast.
7.explain:
“Unleavened bread shall be eaten seven days.”

The command is repeated for emphasis. The bread must be unleavened for the whole week.

“And no leavened bread shall be seen among you, nor shall leaven be seen among you in all your quarters.”

Not only must they avoid eating leaven. None may even be “seen” anywhere in their territory. The word “quarters” refers to their borders, the whole land they occupy.

8.brief: Each father is to tell his son, “This is done because of what the LORD did for me when I came up from Egypt.” Every generation is to speak of the exodus as their own deliverance.
8.explain:
“And you shall tell your son in that day, saying,”

The feast is a teaching occasion. Each father is to “tell your son.” The story of the exodus passes from parent to child.

“This is done because of what the LORD did for me when I came up from Egypt.”

The father speaks in the first person: “what the LORD did for me.” Later generations who never saw Egypt are still to say “me” and “I came up.” Each generation is to speak of the exodus as their own deliverance.
8.notes: The Jewish Passover meal still includes this verse. Each person at the table is taught to regard himself as if he had personally come out of Egypt.

9.brief: The observance is to be a sign on their hand and a memorial between their eyes, so “that the LORD’s law may be in your mouth,” for the LORD brought them out with a strong hand. Remembering God’s deliverance should keep His word on their lips.
9.explain:
“It shall be as a sign to you on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes,”

The feast is to be like “a sign” on the hand and “a memorial between your eyes.” The picture is of something always before them, shaping what they do with their hands and what they keep in view.

“that the LORD’s law may be in your mouth;”

The purpose is to keep God’s law on their lips. Remembering what God did should keep His word on their lips, in their speech and teaching.

“for with a strong hand the LORD has brought you out of Egypt.”

The reason again is the LORD’s “strong hand.” God’s power in the exodus is the foundation for Israel’s obedience.
9.notes: Interpreters differ on whether the sign on the hand and between the eyes is meant figuratively or literally. Later Jewish practice took similar language in Deuteronomy 6:8 and Deuteronomy 11:18 literally and wore small boxes holding Scripture passages, called tefillin or phylacteries. Jesus mentions phylacteries in Matthew 23:5.

10.brief: Israel is to keep this ordinance in its season year after year. The remembrance is to be regular and lasting.
10.explain:
“You shall therefore keep this ordinance in its season from year to year.”

The feast is to be kept “in its season,” at its appointed time, “from year to year.” Remembrance is to be regular and lasting.

11.brief: Moses turns back to the firstborn and speaks of the day when the LORD brings Israel into the land of the Canaanites and gives it to them, as He swore to them and their fathers. The verse sets the time and setting for the command about the firstborn in the next verse.
11.explain:
“And it shall be, when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as He swore to you and your fathers, and gives it to you,”

Moses returns to the firstborn, the subject of 13:1–2. Again he speaks of the land as certain. God “swore” it to the fathers and to the people themselves, and He “gives it.” The command about the firstborn will apply once they live in the land.

12.brief: Israel is to set apart to the LORD every firstborn that opens the womb, and the firstborn males of their animals belong to the LORD. God’s claim on the firstborn becomes part of Israel’s ongoing life.
12.explain:
“that you shall set apart to the LORD all that open the womb,”

Israel is to “set apart to the LORD” every firstborn. The verb reads literally cause to pass over to the LORD. What God spared becomes His.

“that is, every firstborn that comes from an animal which you have; the males shall be the LORD’s.”

The firstborn males of the livestock belong to God. Clean animals, such as cattle, sheep, and goats, were to be sacrificed (Numbers 18:17). God’s claim on the firstborn becomes part of Israel’s ongoing life.

13.brief: Every firstborn donkey is to be redeemed with a lamb or else have its neck broken, and every firstborn son must be redeemed. Firstborn sons are never sacrificed; they are redeemed, because God claims them as His own.
13.explain:
“But every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb;”

A donkey was an unclean animal and could not be offered in sacrifice. Its firstborn had to be redeemed “with a lamb.” To redeem means to buy back by paying a price. The lamb was given in its place.

“and if you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck.”

If the owner would not redeem the donkey, it had to be killed. It could not simply be kept. Either way, God’s claim on the firstborn had to be honored.

“And all the firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.”

Firstborn sons were never to be sacrificed. Every one of them was to be redeemed. God claimed them as His own, and the redemption price acknowledged His claim. This set Israel apart from nations around them that sacrificed children (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31).
13.notes:
Numbers 18:15–16 sets the redemption price for a firstborn son at five shekels of silver, paid when the child was a month old.

Luke records that Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple “to present Him to the Lord,” citing this law of the firstborn (Luke 2:22–24).

14.brief: When a son asks, “What is this?” the father is to answer, “By strength of hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.” The practice of redemption opens the door to telling the story of God’s rescue.
14.explain:
“So it shall be, when your son asks you in time to come, saying, ‘What is this?”

God expects the practice to prompt questions. A child would notice the redemption of the firstborn and ask “What is this?” The question opens the way to teaching.

“that you shall say to him, ‘By strength of hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.”

The answer begins with what God did, not with what Israel did. The father explains the practice by telling the story of God’s rescue.

15.brief: The father explains that when Pharaoh stubbornly refused, the LORD killed all Egypt’s firstborn, so Israel sacrifices the firstborn males of its animals and redeems its firstborn sons. The practice remembers both God’s judgment on Egypt and His sparing of Israel’s firstborn.
15.explain:
“And it came to pass, when Pharaoh was stubborn about letting us go,”

The father explains the background. Pharaoh “was stubborn,” hardening himself against letting Israel go.

“that the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man and the firstborn of beast.”

Because of Pharaoh’s refusal, “the LORD killed all the firstborn” of Egypt. The judgment fell on people and animals alike (12:29).

“Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all males that open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.”

The practice follows from the story. “Therefore” the firstborn male animals are sacrificed, and the firstborn sons are redeemed. The practice remembers both God’s judgment on Egypt and His sparing of Israel’s firstborn.
15.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “was stubborn” means to make hard. It is a different word from the ones used for Pharaoh’s heart in the plague chapters, though it describes the same stubbornness.

16.brief: The practice is a sign on the hand and frontlets between the eyes, “for by strength of hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt.” The section ends, like the one before it, with the LORD’s strong hand.
16.explain:
“It shall be as a sign on your hand and as frontlets between your eyes,”

The language echoes 13:9. “Frontlets” were bands or ornaments worn on the forehead. The practice of redeeming the firstborn is to be as visible and constant a reminder as something worn on the body.

“for by strength of hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt.”

The section closes as the one before it did, with the LORD’s strong hand. The whole practice points back to His power in the exodus.

17.brief: When Pharaoh lets the people go, God does not lead them by the near road through the land of the Philistines, lest they change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt. God chooses the route with care for His people’s weakness.
17.explain:
“Then it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near;”

The narrative resumes with Israel’s route. The shortest road to Canaan ran along the Mediterranean coast through “the land of the Philistines.” It was “near,” but God did not lead them that way.

“for God said, ‘Lest perhaps the people change their minds when they see war, and return to Egypt.”

God gives His reason. The coastal road was guarded by fortresses and would have meant battle. Israel had just come out of slavery and was not ready for war. God knew they might “change their minds” and go back. God chooses the route with care for His people’s weakness.
17.notes: Egypt maintained a line of forts along the coastal road into Canaan, sometimes called the Way of Horus.

18.brief: God leads the people around by way of the wilderness of the Red Sea, and Israel goes up out of Egypt in orderly ranks. The longer road is God’s choice, and the people leave as an organized host.
18.explain:
“So God led the people around by way of the wilderness of the Red Sea.”

God “led the people around,” a longer route through the wilderness toward the Red Sea. The longer road was God’s choice, not a mistake.

“And the children of Israel went up in orderly ranks out of the land of Egypt.”

Israel left “in orderly ranks.” They went out as an organized host, not a fleeing mob.
18.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “in orderly ranks” is understood by many as armed or in battle array. It may be related to the word for “five,” suggesting organization in groups.

On the name “Red Sea,” see the note at 10:19.

19.brief: Moses takes the bones of Joseph, who had made Israel swear, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here with you.” Joseph’s faith in God’s promise is honored as Israel leaves Egypt.
19.explain:
“And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him,”

Moses brings “the bones of Joseph.” Joseph had died in Egypt centuries earlier, and his body had been embalmed and placed in a coffin there (Genesis 50:26).

“for he had placed the children of Israel under solemn oath, saying,”

Before his death, Joseph made Israel swear to take his bones with them when they left.

“God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here with you.”

Joseph was sure that “God will surely visit you.” He knew Egypt was not Israel’s home. His request expressed faith that God would keep His promise to bring them to Canaan. Now, generations later, Moses keeps the oath. Hebrews 11:22 says Joseph “gave instructions concerning his bones” by faith.
19.notes:
Joseph’s bones were finally buried at Shechem, in the land Jacob had bought there (Joshua 24:32; Genesis 33:19).

The verb translated “visit” means to attend to or come to the aid of. It is the same word used in 3:16 and 4:31, where God says He has “visited” His people.

20.brief: Israel journeys from Succoth and camps at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness. The people move step by step toward the place God is leading them.
20.explain:
“So they took their journey from Succoth and camped in Etham at the edge of the wilderness.”

Israel moves from “Succoth” to “Etham at the edge of the wilderness.” They are leaving the settled land of Egypt behind. The exact location of Etham is uncertain.

21.brief: The LORD goes before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead the way and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light. God Himself guides His people day and night.
21.explain:
“And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead the way,”

“The LORD went before them.” God Himself led Israel. By day He appeared in “a pillar of cloud,” a visible column showing the way. Israel did not have to guess the route.

“and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so as to go by day and night.”

By night He went before them “in a pillar of fire” that gave them light. Israel could travel by day or night under God’s guidance. The passage describes this visible guidance without explaining how the cloud and the fire were related. God Himself guides His people day and night.
21.notes: The same pillar appears again at the sea (14:19–20, 24) and stays with Israel to the end of the book (40:34–38; compare Numbers 9:15–23).

22.brief: The LORD does not take away the pillar of cloud by day or the pillar of fire by night from before the people. His guiding presence remains with them continually.
22.explain:
“He did not take away the pillar of cloud by day or the pillar of fire by night from before the people.”

God’s presence did not come and go. He “did not take away” the pillar. Day after day and night after night, it remained before the people. His guiding presence was with them continually.
